content: Newborn infants are capable of experiencing pain. Hospitalized newborns often undergo numerous painful procedures, and even healthy newborns may experience pain during assisted vaginal births (via vacuum extraction or forceps) or during blood sampling for newborn screening tests. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of paracetamol (acetaminophen) for preventing or treating procedural or postoperative pain, as well as pain associated with clinical conditions in neonates. Additionally, the review aimed to assess the effects of different doses and routes of administration (oral, intravenous, or rectal) of paracetamol in this population. The search for relevant studies included databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, Embase, and CINAHL, covering publications up to May 2016. Clinical trial databases, Google Scholar, conference proceedings, and reference lists of retrieved articles were also searched. The review included randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials involving neonates (≤28 days old) who received paracetamol for pain prevention or treatment. Data extraction and analysis were conducted independently by two reviewers using pre-designed forms. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion and consensus. The quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. Nine trials involving 728 infants were included in the review. These trials examined the use of paracetamol for various painful procedures, including heel lancing, assisted vaginal birth, eye examinations for retinopathy of prematurity, and postoperative care. However, the results of these studies could not be combined in meta-analyses due to differences in the painful conditions studied, the interventions compared, and the outcome measures used. In the case of heel lancing, paracetamol did not significantly reduce pain when compared to water, cherry elixir, or EMLA cream (a eutectic mixture of lidocaine and prilocaine). One study found that the Premature Infant Pain Profile (PIPP) score within three minutes of lancing was higher in the paracetamol group compared to the oral glucose group (mean difference [MD] 2.21, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.72 to 3.70; 38 infants). For assisted vaginal births, paracetamol did not reduce modified facies scores (a measure of facial expressions associated with pain) in one study involving 119 infants. In another study of 123 infants, the Échelle de Douleur et d'Inconfort du Nouveau‐Né (EDIN) score at two hours of age was significantly higher in the group that received paracetamol suppositories compared to the placebo group (MD 1.00, 95% CI 0.60 to 1.40). Additionally, when these infants underwent heel lancing at two to three days of age, the Bernese Pain Scale for Neonates scores were higher in the paracetamol group, and these infants cried for a longer duration (MD 19 seconds, 95% CI 14 to 24). For eye examinations, paracetamol did not significantly reduce PIPP scores during the first or last 45 seconds of the examination or at five minutes afterward. In one study involving 81 infants, the PIPP score was significantly higher in the paracetamol group compared to the 24% sucrose group (MD 3.90, 95% CI 2.92 to 4.88). However, in another study of 114 infants, the PIPP score during the eye examination was significantly lower in the paracetamol group compared to the water group (MD −2.70, 95% CI −3.55 to −1.85). In the context of postoperative care following major surgery, infants in the paracetamol group required significantly less morphine over 48 hours compared to those in the morphine group (MD −157 µg/kg, 95% CI −27 to −288). No adverse events were reported in any of the included studies. The quality of evidence, as assessed using the GRADE approach, was low. The authors concluded that the limited and low-quality data available do not provide sufficient evidence to establish the role of paracetamol in reducing pain from procedures in neonates. Furthermore, paracetamol administered after assisted vaginal birth may increase the response to subsequent painful exposures. However, paracetamol may reduce the total need for morphine following major surgery, and further research is warranted to explore this potential benefit.
